1:1.t: "Tent of meeting": the KJV's "tabernacle of the congregation", as in Exodus 27:21. The Hebrew ohel mo'ed means the tent where God meets with His people. "The second month" of the second year is about thirteen months after the exodus (Exodus 40:17).

1:2.t: "One by one": the KJV's "by their polls", meaning by heads.

1:8.t: Nethanel: the KJV spells it Nethaneel here and throughout Numbers.

1:14.t: Deuel: the KJV has Reuel at 2:14, as do most Hebrew manuscripts there. The Hebrew letters d and r look very similar.

1:16.t: "Heads of the clans": the KJV's "heads of thousands". The Hebrew elef usually means "thousand" but can also mean a clan or a military unit; see 1:46 below.

1:51.t: "Outsider": the KJV's "stranger". The Hebrew zar here means anyone not a Levite, and at 3:10 anyone not a priest.

2:2.t: "Banner ... emblems": the KJV's "standard" and "ensign". Each group of three tribes camped under one banner, and each family had its own emblem.

3:3.t: "Ordained": the KJV's "consecrated"; literally "whose hand he filled", as in Exodus 28:41. The phrase may come from placing the first offerings in the new priest's hands.

3:4.t: "Unauthorized fire": the KJV's "strange fire", fire not taken from the altar, or offered in a way God had not commanded; see Leviticus 10:1.
"During the lifetime of": the KJV's "in the sight of".

3:19.t: Izhar: the KJV spells it Izehar here, Izhar in Exodus 6:18.

3:36.t: "Frames ... crossbars ... bases": the KJV's "boards ... bars ... sockets", as in Exodus 26.

3:47.t: KJV: "five shekels apiece by the poll". A gerah is about 0.6 grams; see Exodus 30:13.

3:50.t: KJV: "a thousand three hundred and threescore and five shekels" (1,365 shekels).

4:3.t: The Levites served from thirty to fifty here, but from twenty-five at 8:24. The extra five years may have been for training, or the age may have changed; later David set it at twenty (1 Chronicles 23:24-27).

4:5.t: "Screening curtain": the KJV's "covering vail", the curtain in front of the Most Holy Place.

4:6.t: "Fine leather": the KJV's "badgers' skins". The Hebrew tachash is uncertain; suggestions include dolphin or sea cow skin, or a fine dyed leather. See Exodus 25:5. "Poles": the KJV's "staves".

4:7.t: "Table of the Presence": the KJV's "table of shewbread", the table for the bread set before God, literally "bread of the face"; see Exodus 25:30. "Pitchers for drink offerings": the KJV's "covers to cover withal", as in Exodus 25:29.

4:10.t: "Carrying frame": the KJV's "a bar". The Hebrew mot means a pole or frame for carrying.

4:12.t: "Carrying frame": the KJV's "a bar". The Hebrew mot means a pole or frame for carrying.

4:20.t: "While the holy things are being covered": the Hebrew says literally "as a swallowing", which most modern Bibles take to mean "even for a moment". The KJV understands it of the moment the holy things are wrapped (verses 5-15).

5:2.t: "Serious skin disease": the KJV's "leper". The Hebrew tsara'at covers a range of skin conditions and is not the same as modern leprosy (Hansen's disease); see Leviticus 13:2. "Contact with a dead body": the KJV's "defiled by the dead"; compare 19:11-16.

5:8.t: "Close relative": the Hebrew go'el, the family redeemer, the relative who bought back land, freed a kinsman from slavery, or avenged his blood; see Exodus 6:6.

5:10.t: "Each man's holy gifts are his own to give": the KJV's "every man's hallowed things shall be his". Holy gifts belong to the giver until he gives them; once given, they belong to the priest.

5:15.t: KJV: "the tenth part of an ephah of barley meal". Barley was cheaper than wheat, and the offering had no oil or incense because it was not a joyful one.

5:18.t: "Loosen her hair": the KJV's "uncover the woman's head". The Hebrew may mean either; loosened hair was also a sign of mourning or shame (Leviticus 10:6, 13:45).

5:21.t: "Thigh waste away and belly swell": the KJV's "thigh to rot, and thy belly to swell". Many modern Bibles take "thigh" as a polite word for the reproductive organs and read "make your womb miscarry" or "make you unable to have children", which fits verse 28.

5:27.t: "Thigh waste away and belly swell": the KJV's "thigh to rot, and thy belly to swell". Many modern Bibles take "thigh" as a polite word for the reproductive organs and read "make your womb miscarry" or "make you unable to have children", which fits verse 28.

6:2.t: "Nazirite": the KJV spells it "Nazarite", which is easy to confuse with "Nazarene", a person from Nazareth. The two words are unrelated.

"Nazirite" (Hebrew nazir, from nazar, "to separate" or "to consecrate"): a Nazirite was a man or woman who took a vow to be set apart to the LORD for a time. The vow had three marks: no grape products, no haircut, and no contact with the dead. The uncut hair was the visible sign (6:7, "consecration", nezer, the same word used of a king's crown and the high priest's gold plate, Exodus 29:6). Samson (Judges 13:5) and probably Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11) were Nazirites from birth, and Paul seems to have joined in a Nazirite vow (Acts 18:18, 21:23-26). Leviticus 25:5 uses the same word for an unpruned vine.

6:3.t: "Strong drink": beer or other fermented drink, not distilled liquor, which did not yet exist. "Grape juice": the KJV's "liquor of grapes".

6:4.t: "Seeds ... skins": the meaning of the two rare Hebrew words is uncertain; some reverse them.

6:9.t: "The hair he has consecrated": the KJV's "the head of his consecration".

6:20.t: "The breast that was waved and the thigh that was presented": the KJV's "the wave breast and heave shoulder". The Hebrew shoq means the upper hind leg, and the "heave" portion was lifted up and set apart for God and the priests; see Leviticus 7:32-34.

6:21.t: "Whatever else he can afford": the KJV's "that that his hand shall get".

7:13.t: KJV: "an hundred and thirty shekels" and "seventy shekels". 7:14 KJV: "ten shekels of gold". The same weights recur for each tribe.
"Plate ... sprinkling bowl ... dish": the KJV's "charger ... bowl ... spoon". The Hebrew kaf, "palm", means a small pan shaped like an open hand.

7:85.t: KJV: "two thousand and four hundred shekels" of silver and "an hundred and twenty shekels" of gold.

7:89.t: "Him": the KJV reads "to speak with him ... unto him", meaning the LORD. In this verse the voice speaks from the place God had promised to meet with Moses (Exodus 25:22).

8:2.t: "Light up the area in front of the lampstand": the KJV's "give light over against the candlestick". The lamps were turned to shine forward.

8:4.t: "From its base to its blossoms": the KJV's "unto the shaft thereof, unto the flowers thereof", meaning from top to bottom.

8:7.t: "Water of purification": the KJV's "water of purifying", literally "water of sin", water for removing sin's defilement; compare 19:9.

8:11.t: "Present ... as an offering": the Hebrew is tenuphah, "wave offering", the word used for portions lifted before the LORD (Leviticus 7:30). The Levites were not waved, of course; the word marks them as given to God and then given by Him to the priests (8:19).

8:13.t: "Present ... as an offering": the Hebrew is tenuphah, "wave offering", the word used for portions lifted before the LORD (Leviticus 7:30). The Levites were not waved, of course; the word marks them as given to God and then given by Him to the priests (8:19).

8:15.t: "Present ... as an offering": the Hebrew is tenuphah, "wave offering", the word used for portions lifted before the LORD (Leviticus 7:30). The Levites were not waved, of course; the word marks them as given to God and then given by Him to the priests (8:19).

8:21.t: "Present ... as an offering": the Hebrew is tenuphah, "wave offering", the word used for portions lifted before the LORD (Leviticus 7:30). The Levites were not waved, of course; the word marks them as given to God and then given by Him to the priests (8:19).

8:16.t: "The first son born to every Israelite woman": the KJV's "such as open every womb"; compare Exodus 13:12.

9:3.t: "At twilight": the KJV's "at even"; the Hebrew is "between the two evenings", as in Exodus 12:6.

9:5.t: "At twilight": the KJV's "at even"; the Hebrew is "between the two evenings", as in Exodus 12:6.

9:11.t: "At twilight": the KJV's "at even"; the Hebrew is "between the two evenings", as in Exodus 12:6.
"The lamb": supplied for clarity; the KJV has "it". The second-month Passover gave those who were unclean or away a second chance to keep it. Hezekiah later used this rule (2 Chronicles 30:2-3).

9:12.t: "Do not ... break any of its bones": see Exodus 12:46 and John 19:36.

9:13.t: "Cut off" (Hebrew karat): the phrase may mean being put to death, being expelled from the community, or God Himself ending the person's line. The Law does not say which in each case. See Exodus 12:15.

10:2.t: "Hammered silver": the KJV's "of a whole piece", hammered out of a single piece of silver.

10:4.t: "Heads of the clans": the KJV's "heads of the thousands". The Hebrew elef usually means "thousand" but can also mean a clan or a military unit; see 1:46.

10:5.t: "Signal blast": the KJV's "an alarm". The Hebrew teru'ah is a loud, rising blast or shout. The Greek Old Testament adds the west and north camps in verse 6.

10:21.t: "Holy things": the KJV's "the sanctuary", meaning the holy furnishings. "Before they arrived": the KJV's "against they came", so that the tabernacle was standing when the holy things reached the new camp.

10:29.t: Reuel: the KJV spells it Raguel here, as in the Greek; Exodus 2:18 has Reuel. The Hebrew can be read so that Hobab, not Reuel, is Moses' father-in-law, as Judges 4:11 says; the KJV links the title to Reuel.

10:36.t: "Countless thousands": the KJV's "the many thousands", literally "ten thousands of thousands".

11:1.t: "Complained": the KJV's wording. The Hebrew adds that they complained "as those suffering hardship", or "of evil".

11:4.t: "Mixed crowd": the KJV's "mixt multitude", people who were not descended from Jacob, Egyptians and others, who left Egypt with Israel; see Exodus 12:38. "Crave other food": the KJV's "fell a lusting", a strong craving.

11:6.t: "Appetite": the KJV's "soul" (Hebrew nephesh, which can mean throat or appetite; see Genesis 2:7).

11:7.t: Bdellium is a pale, sweet-smelling gum resin; compare Genesis 2:12.

11:8.t: "Something made with fresh olive oil": the KJV's "the taste of fresh oil". Exodus 16:31 says it tasted like wafers made with honey.

11:12.t: "In your arms": the KJV's "in thy bosom". "A nurse": the KJV's "a nursing father".

11:20.t: "You have rejected": the KJV's "ye have despised".

11:23.t: "Is the LORD's arm too short?": the KJV's "Is the LORD's hand waxed short?", meaning, is His power limited?

11:28.t: "One of his chosen young men": the KJV's "one of his young men". Many modern Bibles read the Hebrew as "from his youth".

11:29.t: "Are you jealous for my sake?": the KJV's "Enviest thou for my sake?"

11:31.t: KJV: "two cubits high". The Hebrew may mean the quail were piled that deep, or that they flew about that high above the ground, low enough to catch.

12:1.t: "Cushite": the KJV's "Ethiopian", its usual rendering of the Hebrew Cush, a land south of Egypt; see Genesis 2:13. Whether this was Zipporah (Exodus 2:21) or a second wife is not said.

12:8.t: "Face to face": the KJV's "mouth to mouth". "Plainly": the KJV's "apparently", meaning openly, not "seemingly". "Riddles": the KJV's "dark speeches". "Form": the KJV's "similitude"; compare Exodus 33:20-23.

12:10.t: "A serious skin disease": the KJV's "leprous". The Hebrew tsara'at covers a range of skin conditions and is not the same as modern leprosy (Hansen's disease); see Leviticus 13:2.

12:14.t: "Spit in her face": a sign of public shame (Deuteronomy 25:9).

13:8.t: Hoshea: the KJV's "Oshea". Hoshea means "salvation"; Joshua (the KJV's "Jehoshua") means "the LORD saves". See Exodus 14:13.

13:16.t: Hoshea: the KJV's "Oshea". Hoshea means "salvation"; Joshua (the KJV's "Jehoshua") means "the LORD saves". See Exodus 14:13.

13:17.t: "The south": the Negev, the dry region in the south of Canaan, as in Genesis 12:9.

13:22.t: "The south": the Negev, the dry region in the south of Canaan, as in Genesis 12:9.
"Descendants of Anak": the KJV's "children of Anak", a people known for their great height (Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 9:2).

13:29.t: "The south": the Negev, the dry region in the south of Canaan, as in Genesis 12:9.

13:19.t: "Open camps or fortified": the KJV's "in tents, or in strong holds".

13:21.t: Lebo-hamath: the KJV's "as men come to Hamath". It may be a place name, Lebo of Hamath, or mean "the entrance to Hamath".

13:23.t: "Valley": the KJV's "brook". The Hebrew nachal is a valley with a stream that may run only in the rainy season. Eshcol means "cluster".

13:32.t: "Devours those who live in it": a land hard to hold, perhaps because of constant war, or a land that wore out its people.

"Bad report" (Hebrew dibbah): the KJV's "evil report". Dibbah means a whispered, damaging report, a slander or rumor, not simply bad news. The spies had first reported honestly (13:27-29); now they spread a distorted account to turn the people against going in. 14:36 calls it "slander" in the KJV. The same word describes Joseph's bad report about his brothers (Genesis 37:2).

14:9.t: "We will eat them up like bread": the KJV's "they are bread for us". "Protection": the KJV's "defence", literally "shade", the shelter of their gods.

14:11.t: "Treat Me with contempt": the KJV's "provoke me". The Hebrew na'ats means to despise or spurn.

"Believe in Me" (Hebrew he'emin): to trust, to rely on God as firm and reliable, from the same root as amen. It is the same verb as Genesis 15:6, "Abram believed the LORD". Hebrews 3:16-19 draws on this chapter: "they could not enter because of unbelief."

14:23.t: "Treat Me with contempt": the KJV's "provoke me". The Hebrew na'ats means to despise or spurn.

14:22.t: "These ten times": possibly a round number for "again and again"; compare Genesis 31:7.

14:25.t: "Red Sea": here probably the Gulf of Aqaba. The Hebrew is yam suph, "Sea of Reeds"; the KJV follows the Greek Old Testament in calling it the Red Sea. See Exodus 10:19.

14:33.t: "Wander": the KJV's wording. The Hebrew says "be shepherds", living as herdsmen moving from pasture to pasture. "Unfaithfulness": the KJV's "whoredoms"; the Old Testament often pictures turning from God as unfaithfulness in marriage (see Exodus 34:15-16).

14:34.t: "What it means when I withdraw My promise": the KJV's "my breach of promise". The Hebrew tenu'ah is rare; it probably means "My opposition", what it is to have God against you. The KJV margin gives "altering of my purpose".

14:45.t: "Beat them down": the KJV's "discomfited them". Hormah means "destruction" (see 21:3).

15:3.t: "Food offerings": the KJV's "an offering made by fire". The Hebrew word (isheh) may be related to "fire" or to a word for "gift"; see Leviticus 1:9. "Pleasing aroma": the KJV's "sweet savour", meaning the offering is accepted by God, not that God needs food; see Exodus 29:18.

15:4.t: KJV: "a tenth deal of flour" with "the fourth part of an hin of oil" and of wine (lamb); "two tenth deals" with "the third part of an hin" (ram); "three tenth deals" with "half an hin" (bull).

15:20.t: "Loaf": the KJV's "cake". "Contribution": the KJV's "heave offering", a portion lifted up and set apart for God and the priests; see Leviticus 7:14.

15:25.t: "Mistake": the KJV's "ignorance", as throughout verses 24-29. The Hebrew bishgagah covers sins committed by mistake or without realizing it was a sin, as opposed to defiant sin "with a high hand" (15:30). See Leviticus 4:2.

15:32.t: "Wood": the KJV's "sticks". Gathering wood for a fire was work forbidden on the Sabbath (Exodus 35:3).

16:1.t: "Took men": the KJV's wording; the Hebrew says only "took", with no object. Many modern Bibles read "became insolent" or "took action".

Korah: a Levite of the Kohathite clan, cousin of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:18-21). The rebellion joins two complaints: Korah's Levites wanted the priesthood (16:10), and the Reubenites Dathan and Abiram, from the tribe of Jacob's firstborn, resented Moses' leadership (16:13). Korah's own sons did not die (26:11), and their descendants became temple singers; eleven psalms are titled "of the sons of Korah" (Psalms 42, 44-49, 84-85, 87-88). Jude 11 names "the rebellion of Korah" as a warning.

16:2.t: "Chosen from the assembly": the KJV's "famous in the congregation"; literally "called ones of the assembly", men summoned to the council.

16:3.t: "You have gone too far": the KJV's "Ye take too much upon you". Moses throws their own words back at them in verse 7.

"The whole community is holy": Korah's claim echoes God's call for Israel to be holy (Exodus 19:6, 15:40). His mistake was to conclude that no one could be set apart for special service. Holiness is God's gift, and He chooses who may come near (16:5).

16:7.t: "You have gone too far": the KJV's "Ye take too much upon you". Moses throws their own words back at them in verse 7.

16:14.t: "Gouge out the eyes of these men": an idiom meaning "deceive" or "blind them to the truth".

16:15.t: "Do not accept their offering": the KJV's "Respect not thou their offering", as in Genesis 4:4-5.

16:24.t: "Tents": the KJV's "tabernacle", here meaning their dwelling.

16:27.t: "Tents": the KJV's "tabernacle", here meaning their dwelling.

16:29.t: "Suffer the fate of all mankind": the KJV's "be visited after the visitation of all men".

16:36.t: In the Hebrew Bible these verses are 17:1-15, and 17:1-13 is 17:16-28. We follow the KJV's numbering.

16:37.t: "Coals": the KJV's "fire". 16:38 "Who sinned at the cost of their lives": the KJV's "these sinners against their own souls".

16:38.t: "Sheets to cover the altar": the KJV's "broad plates for a covering of the altar". The bronze altar was already overlaid (Exodus 27:2); this was an added covering as a reminder.

16:40.t: "Outsider": the KJV's "stranger". The Hebrew zar here means anyone not a priest descended from Aaron; see 1:51.

17:2.t: "Staffs": the KJV's "rods", as in Exodus 4:2. Each tribal leader's staff was the sign of his authority; the Hebrew matteh also means "tribe".

17:7.t: "Tent of the Testimony": the KJV's "tabernacle of witness".

17:10.t: Hebrews 9:4 says Aaron's staff was kept in the ark.

18:1.t: "Bear the responsibility for offenses": the KJV's "bear the iniquity". The priests were answerable for any wrong done in the sanctuary.

18:7.t: "Behind the curtain": the KJV's "within the vail". "As a gift": the KJV's "as a service of gift".

18:8.t: "Portion": the KJV's "by reason of the anointing". The Hebrew word may mean either "anointing" or "share".

18:9.t: "Kept back from the fire": the part not burned on the altar.

18:10.t: "In the most holy place": the KJV's wording. It does not mean the inner room behind the curtain, but a most holy area, the courtyard of the tent of meeting (Leviticus 6:16).

18:12.t: "New wine": the KJV's "wine"; the Hebrew tirosh means freshly pressed wine.

18:14.t: "Devoted": the Hebrew cherem, something handed over entirely to God, which could not be kept for personal use or bought back; see Exodus 22:20 and Leviticus 27:28.

18:15.t: "The first offspring of every womb": the KJV's "every thing that openeth the matrix"; see Exodus 13:12.

18:16.t: KJV: "five shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs".

18:18.t: "The right thigh": the KJV's "right shoulder". The Hebrew shoq means the upper hind leg; see Leviticus 7:32.

18:27.t: "Grain": the KJV's "corn", which meant grain of any kind.

18:30.t: "Grain": the KJV's "corn", which meant grain of any kind.

19:2.t: "A requirement of the law": the KJV's "the ordinance of the law".

"Red heifer" (Hebrew parah adummah): a young cow, reddish-brown in color, never yoked for work. Red may recall blood, the sign of life. Unlike other sacrifices, she was killed outside the camp and burned whole, and her ashes, mixed with water, cleansed people from contact with death, the strongest source of uncleanness. Hebrews 9:13-14 compares "the ashes of a heifer" with the blood of Christ, which cleanses the conscience. Jewish tradition counted this law among the hardest to understand, since the ashes made the unclean clean but made those who handled them unclean.

19:3.t: "She is to be taken ... and slaughtered": the KJV's "that he may bring her forth without the camp, and one shall slay her". The Hebrew says "he shall bring her out ... and one shall slaughter her", so someone other than Eleazar may have done the killing.

19:9.t: "Water for cleansing": the KJV's "water of separation". The Hebrew mei niddah, "water of impurity", means the water that removes impurity.

"Purification from sin" (Hebrew chatta't): the KJV's "a purification for sin". The word is the one used for the sin offering; see Exodus 29:14 and Leviticus 15:31. Here it means a purification offering, removing the defilement of death, not punishment for a moral wrong.

19:13.t: "Water for cleansing": the KJV's "water of separation". The Hebrew mei niddah, "water of impurity", means the water that removes impurity.

19:20.t: "Water for cleansing": the KJV's "water of separation". The Hebrew mei niddah, "water of impurity", means the water that removes impurity.

19:15.t: "Lid fastened on it": the KJV's "covering bound upon it".

19:17.t: "Burned purification offering": the KJV's "the burnt heifer of purification for sin". "Fresh water": the KJV's "running water", literally "living water", as at Leviticus 14:5.

20:1.t: "The first month": the year is not given. Aaron's death later in this chapter came in the fortieth year (33:38), so this is probably near the end of the wilderness years.

20:14.t: "Hardships": the KJV's "travail". Edom descended from Esau, Jacob's brother, so Israel calls itself Edom's brother.

20:17.t: "The King's Highway": the KJV's "the king's high way", the main trade route running north and south east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea.

20:24.t: "Gathered to his people": a way of speaking of death, being joined to one's ancestors (Genesis 25:8).

20:26.t: "Gathered to his people": a way of speaking of death, being joined to one's ancestors (Genesis 25:8).

21:1.t: "Negev": the KJV's "the south". "The road of the spies": the KJV's reading. The Hebrew atarim may instead be a place name, "the road to Atharim", as many modern Bibles take it.

21:3.t: Hormah sounds like the Hebrew cherem, "devoted to destruction".

21:4.t: "Grew impatient": the KJV's "the soul of the people was much discouraged", literally "their soul was short".

21:5.t: "Miserable food": the KJV's "light bread", meaning the manna. The Hebrew qeloqel means worthless or contemptible.

21:6.t: "Fiery snakes": the KJV's "fiery serpents". The Hebrew seraphim, "burning ones", may describe the burning pain of their venom or their color. The same word names the heavenly beings in Isaiah 6:2.

21:11.t: Iye-abarim: the KJV spells it Ije-abarim. 21:12 "The Zered Valley": the KJV's "the valley of Zared". 21:32 Jazer: the KJV spells it Jaazer here.

21:14.t: "The Book of the Wars of the LORD": a lost collection of songs about Israel's battles. "What He did at the Red Sea" follows the KJV. The Hebrew reads "Vaheb in Suphah", probably names of a town and a region, and many modern Bibles print it that way.

21:18.t: "Under the direction of the lawgiver": the KJV's reading. The Hebrew mechoqeq can mean a lawgiver or a ruler's staff, and many modern Bibles read "with the scepter".

21:20.t: "The wasteland": the KJV's "Jeshimon", which may be a place name or the Hebrew word for desert.

21:24.t: "Strongly defended": the KJV's "strong". The Greek Old Testament reads "Jazer was the border of the Ammonites".

21:27.t: "The poets": the KJV's "they that speak in proverbs". The Hebrew moshelim means those who recite sayings or ballads. Verses 27-30 are an Amorite victory song over Moab, now turned to celebrate Israel's victory over the Amorites.

21:29.t: Chemosh was the national god of Moab (1 Kings 11:7).

22:1.t: "On the east side of the Jordan across from Jericho": the KJV's "on this side Jordan by Jericho". "This side" is spoken from the land of Canaan; the plains of Moab lie east of the river.

22:5.t: "The River": the Euphrates. "In the land of his own people": the KJV's "the land of the children of his people". Some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions read "the land of the Ammonites", and some take the Hebrew as "the land of Amaw", a region near the Euphrates.

22:7.t: "The fee for divination": the KJV's "the rewards of divination". 2 Peter 2:15 says Balaam "loved the wages of wrongdoing".

22:8.t: "Officials": the KJV's "princes", here and throughout these chapters.

22:18.t: "Anything, great or small": the KJV's "to do less or more".

22:22.t: "To oppose him": the KJV's "for an adversary against him". The Hebrew word is satan, "adversary", used here of the LORD's angel, not of the devil.

22:32.t: "Perverse": the Hebrew word is rare; it may mean reckless or headlong.

22:39.t: Kiriath-huzoth: the KJV spells it Kirjath-huzoth. The name means "town of streets".

23:3.t: "A bare hilltop": the KJV's "an high place". The Hebrew shephi means a bare height.

23:7.t: "Oracle" (Hebrew mashal): the KJV's "parable". Mashal means a saying, proverb, comparison or poem, any carefully shaped speech. Balaam's seven oracles in chapters 23-24 are poems.

23:10.t: "A fourth of Israel": the KJV's "the fourth part of Israel". The Hebrew rova may instead mean "dust cloud", matching "the dust of Jacob".

23:14.t: "The field of Zophim": the name means "field of watchmen", a lookout point.

23:21.t: "Trouble": the KJV's "perverseness". The Hebrew amal can mean trouble, misery or wrongdoing.

"He has not looked on wickedness in Jacob": this does not mean Israel had no sin, as the next chapter shows. It means God would not allow a curse to fall on the people He had chosen and blessed. "The shout of a king" is the people's acclaim of the LORD as their King.

23:22.t: "Wild ox": the KJV's "unicorn". The Hebrew re'em is a wild ox, probably the now extinct aurochs. The Greek Old Testament translated it "one-horned", and the KJV followed it.

24:8.t: "Wild ox": the KJV's "unicorn". The Hebrew re'em is a wild ox, probably the now extinct aurochs. The Greek Old Testament translated it "one-horned", and the KJV followed it.

23:23.t: "Against Jacob": the KJV's reading. The Hebrew can also mean "in Jacob", that is, Israel does not use sorcery. "See what God has done!": the KJV's "What hath God wrought!", the words Samuel Morse sent in the first long-distance telegraph message in 1844.

23:24.t: "Lioness ... lion": the KJV's "great lion ... young lion". Hebrew has several words for lions, and their exact differences are uncertain.

24:1.t: "Omens": the KJV's "enchantments", signs a diviner looked for.

24:3.t: "The message of": the KJV's "hath said". The Hebrew ne'um is the word used for a prophet's solemn declaration. "Falls down": the KJV adds "into a trance", which is not in the Hebrew.
"Whose eyes are open": the Hebrew word is rare and may instead mean "whose eye is closed".

24:15.t: "The message of": the KJV's "hath said". The Hebrew ne'um is the word used for a prophet's solemn declaration. "Falls down": the KJV adds "into a trance", which is not in the Hebrew.

24:6.t: "Aloes": the KJV's "lign aloes", a fragrant tree.

24:7.t: "Agag": the KJV's reading, as in the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament reads "Gog". A later Amalekite king named Agag was defeated by Saul (1 Samuel 15:8).

24:11.t: "Get out of here and go home": the KJV's "flee thou to thy place". "Reward you richly": the KJV's "promote thee unto great honour".

24:14.t: "Warn you": the KJV's "advertise thee", meaning inform. "In the days to come": the KJV's "in the latter days".

24:17.t: "Borders": the KJV's "corners". The Hebrew may mean the sides of the head, that is, the forehead. "The sons of Sheth": the KJV's reading. Sheth may be the tribe's ancestor, or the Hebrew may mean "the sons of tumult"; Jeremiah 48:45 reads "the sons of uproar".

"A Star will come out of Jacob, and a Scepter will rise out of Israel" (Hebrew kokhav, shevet): a star often stood for a king, and the scepter is a ruler's staff (Genesis 49:10). The first fulfillment was David, who conquered Moab and Edom (2 Samuel 8:2, 8:14). Jewish and Christian readers alike came to read it of the Messiah; the leader of the Jewish revolt of A.D. 132 was called Bar Kokhba, "son of the star". Many Christians link it with the star the Magi followed (Matthew 2:2) and with Jesus, "the bright morning star" (Revelation 22:16).

24:18.t: "Conquered": the KJV's "a possession". Seir is the hill country of Edom.

24:21.t: The name Kenite sounds like the Hebrew qen, "nest". Asshur is Assyria.

24:24.t: Kittim: the KJV spells it Chittim. It was Cyprus, and later stood for peoples of the west. Eber may mean the Hebrews or peoples beyond the Euphrates.

25:1.t: "Shittim": the name means "acacia trees". "Commit sexual immorality": the KJV's "commit whoredom". The women's gods were part of the seduction (25:2), and 31:16 says it was Balaam's advice.

25:4.t: "Hang them up ... in broad daylight": the KJV's "hang them up before the LORD against the sun". The Hebrew verb may mean to execute by impaling or to expose the bodies after execution. The leaders who had led the people astray were to be publicly punished.

25:6.t: "Relatives": the KJV's "brethren". "Weeping": the people were mourning over the plague (25:8-9).

25:8.t: "The inner tent": the KJV's "the tent". The Hebrew qubbah, used only here, may mean an alcove or a sacred tent used for pagan rites.

25:9.t: Paul gives the number as twenty-three thousand (1 Corinthians 10:8), perhaps counting those who died in one day, or rounding differently.

25:14.t: "The leader of a family": the KJV's "a prince of a chief house".

25:17.t: "Treat ... as enemies": the KJV's "Vex ... they vex you".

26:2.t: "By their families": the KJV's "throughout their fathers' house", the ancestral family groups.

26:4.t: "Take a census of the men": the KJV's "Take the sum of the people"; "the people" is supplied in italics. Many modern Bibles end the command at "Moses" and read the rest as a heading: "The Israelites who came out of Egypt were these".

26:5.t: "Clan": the KJV's "family". Several names differ from the lists in Genesis 46 and Exodus 6: Nemuel is Jemuel there, Zephon is Ziphion, Ozni is Ezbon, Arod is Arodi, Shuham is Hushim, and Shupham and Hupham are Muppim and Huppim.

26:9.t: "Well known in the community": the KJV's "famous in the congregation". The Hebrew means "called by the community", that is, chosen as its representatives (1:16, 16:2).

26:11.t: The sons of Korah survived, and their descendants became temple singers; eleven psalms bear their name (Psalms 42-49, 84-85, 87-88).

26:13.t: Zerahite: the KJV's "Zarhites". 26:20-21 Perez, Perezite: the KJV's "Pharez, Pharzites". 26:23 Puah: the KJV spells it Pua. 26:26 Seredite: the KJV's "Sardites". 26:30 Iezer, Iezerite: the KJV's "Jeezer, Jeezerites". 26:35 Shuthelahite, Becherite: the KJV's "Shuthalhites, Bachrites". 26:44 Imnah, Ishvi: the KJV's "Jimna, Jesui". 26:46 Serah: the KJV spells it Sarah here. 26:58 Korahite: the KJV's "Korathites".

26:20.t: Zerahite: the KJV's "Zarhites". 26:20-21 Perez, Perezite: the KJV's "Pharez, Pharzites". 26:23 Puah: the KJV spells it Pua. 26:26 Seredite: the KJV's "Sardites". 26:30 Iezer, Iezerite: the KJV's "Jeezer, Jeezerites". 26:35 Shuthelahite, Becherite: the KJV's "Shuthalhites, Bachrites". 26:44 Imnah, Ishvi: the KJV's "Jimna, Jesui". 26:46 Serah: the KJV spells it Sarah here. 26:58 Korahite: the KJV's "Korathites".

26:51.t: The total, 601,730, is 1,820 fewer than at the first census (1:46).

26:61.t: "Unauthorized fire": the KJV's "strange fire", fire not taken from the altar, or offered in a way God had not commanded. See Leviticus 10:1.

27:3.t: "He died because of his own sin": he died like the rest of his generation, under the judgment of 14:29, not in Korah's rebellion, which might have cost his family its land.

27:11.t: "Legal requirement": the KJV's "a statute of judgment".

27:12.t: "This mountain in the Abarim range": the KJV's "this mount Abarim". Abarim means "the regions beyond", the mountains east of the Jordan; the peak is Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 32:49, 34:1).

27:16.t: "The God of the spirits of all mankind" (Hebrew elohei haruchot lekhol basar): the same title appears at 16:22. God gives life and breath (ruach) to every person and knows every heart, so He can choose the right leader. See Genesis 1:2 on ruach.

27:17.t: "Go out ... come in": a Hebrew way of saying "lead in everything", especially in war.
"Sheep without a shepherd": Jesus saw the crowds "like sheep without a shepherd" and had compassion on them (Matthew 9:36, Mark 6:34). In Greek, Joshua's name is Iesous, Jesus.

27:20.t: "Authority": the KJV's "honour". The Hebrew hod means splendor or majesty.

28:2.t: "My food": the KJV's "my bread", as at Leviticus 21:6. It means the offerings, not that God eats.

"At the appointed time" (Hebrew bemo'ado): from mo'adim, times set by God for meeting with His people, the same root as ohel mo'ed, "tent of meeting" (see Leviticus 23:2). Chapters 28-29 set out, day by day through the year, the public offerings for the whole nation: daily, weekly, monthly and at each festival. Leviticus 23 told the people what days to keep; these chapters tell the priests what to offer on them.

28:3.t: "Regular burnt offering": the KJV's "continual burnt offering", offered every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38-42).

"Regular" (Hebrew tamid, "continual"): the daily morning and evening offering was never to stop, so that Israel's worship went on without a break. Daniel speaks of a time when the tamid would be taken away (Daniel 8:11). Hebrews 10:11-14 contrasts these daily, repeated sacrifices with Christ's single offering.

28:4.t: "At twilight": the KJV's "at even", literally "between the two evenings".

28:8.t: "At twilight": the KJV's "at even", literally "between the two evenings".

28:5.t: KJV: "a tenth part of an ephah of flour" and "the fourth part of an hin of beaten oil". 28:7 KJV: "the fourth part of an hin".

28:7.t: "Fermented drink": the KJV's "strong wine". The Hebrew shekar is usually "strong drink", here meaning wine.

28:9.t: KJV: "two tenth deals", "three tenth deals" and "a several tenth deal", that is, two tenths, three tenths and one tenth of an ephah.

28:12.t: KJV: "two tenth deals", "three tenth deals" and "a several tenth deal", that is, two tenths, three tenths and one tenth of an ephah.

28:20.t: KJV: "two tenth deals", "three tenth deals" and "a several tenth deal", that is, two tenths, three tenths and one tenth of an ephah.

28:28.t: KJV: "two tenth deals", "three tenth deals" and "a several tenth deal", that is, two tenths, three tenths and one tenth of an ephah.

28:14.t: KJV: "half an hin", "the third part of an hin" and "a fourth part of an hin".

28:18.t: "Sacred assembly ... regular work": the KJV's "holy convocation ... servile work". A sacred assembly (Hebrew miqra qodesh) is a holy gathering called by proclamation, a day when ordinary work stopped. See Leviticus 23:2, 23:7.

28:25.t: "Sacred assembly ... regular work": the KJV's "holy convocation ... servile work". A sacred assembly (Hebrew miqra qodesh) is a holy gathering called by proclamation, a day when ordinary work stopped. See Leviticus 23:2, 23:7.

28:26.t: "After your seven weeks are completed": the KJV's "after your weeks be out". The Hebrew can also be read "at your Festival of Weeks", as many modern Bibles take it; see Leviticus 23:15-16.

29:1.t: "A day for you to sound the trumpets": the KJV's "a day of blowing the trumpets". The Hebrew teru'ah means a loud blast or shout; the instrument was probably the ram's horn. See Leviticus 23:24.

29:3.t: KJV: "three tenth deals", "two tenth deals" and "one tenth deal" (or "a several tenth deal") of flour, tenths of an ephah.

29:9.t: KJV: "three tenth deals", "two tenth deals" and "one tenth deal" (or "a several tenth deal") of flour, tenths of an ephah.

29:14.t: KJV: "three tenth deals", "two tenth deals" and "one tenth deal" (or "a several tenth deal") of flour, tenths of an ephah.

29:7.t: "Humble yourselves": the KJV's "afflict your souls", which came to mean fasting (Psalm 35:13, Isaiah 58:3). This is the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur; see Leviticus 16:29.

29:11.t: "The sin offering for atonement": the special offering of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).

29:12.t: The Festival of Booths (Leviticus 23:34). The number of bulls drops by one each day, from thirteen to seven, seventy in all over the seven days.

29:35.t: "Closing assembly": the KJV's "solemn assembly". The Hebrew atseret comes from a verb meaning to hold back or close. See Leviticus 23:36.

29:40.t: In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 30:1, and 30:1-16 is 30:2-17.

30:2.t: "Bind himself": the KJV's "bind his soul", here meaning himself (nephesh), and so throughout this chapter.

"Vow ... oath ... pledge" (Hebrew neder, shevu'ah, issar): a neder was a promise to give or do something for God, often on condition that He answered a prayer (21:2, Genesis 28:20-22). An issar, "binding", was a pledge to hold back from something, such as food. Once spoken to God, a vow had to be kept (Deuteronomy 23:21-23, Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). Jesus warned against using oaths to dodge the truth (Matthew 5:33-37).

30:5.t: "Release her": the KJV's "forgive her". She is not guilty of breaking her vow.

30:8.t: "Release her": the KJV's "forgive her". She is not guilty of breaking her vow.

30:12.t: "Release her": the KJV's "forgive her". She is not guilty of breaking her vow.

30:6.t: "Rash promise": the KJV's "uttered ought out of her lips". The Hebrew mivta suggests something said thoughtlessly (Leviticus 5:4).

"If she has a husband when she makes a vow": the KJV's reading. Many modern Bibles read "if she marries while under a vow", taking verses 6-8 as vows made before marriage and verses 10-15 as vows made during it.

30:13.t: "To humble herself": the KJV's "to afflict the soul", usually by fasting or self-denial. See Leviticus 16:29.

30:15.t: "Bear her guilt": the KJV's "bear her iniquity". If he cancels a vow he had already let stand, the guilt for the broken vow is his, not hers.

31:6.t: "The holy objects": the KJV's "the holy instruments". They may have been the ark or other sacred items carried into battle (compare 10:9, Joshua 6:4).

31:7.t: "Every male": the men of the Midianites in this region. Midianites appear again in Judges 6, so the people as a whole were not wiped out.

31:8.t: The Midianite kings are called "princes of Sihon" in Joshua 13:21. Balaam had not gone home after all (24:25), or had returned to advise Midian (31:16).

31:10.t: "Encampments": the KJV's "goodly castles". The Hebrew tirah means a walled camp or settlement.

31:16.t: "On Balaam's advice": the KJV's "through the counsel of Balaam". Chapter 25 does not say this; here we learn that Balaam, who could not curse Israel, showed Moab and Midian how to lead Israel into sin (Revelation 2:14).

31:17.t: These verses are among the hardest in the Old Testament for modern readers. The women who had led Israel into idolatry at Peor were judged; the girls were spared and were to live as part of Israel, under the laws that protected captive women (Deuteronomy 21:10-14).

31:23.t: "Water for cleansing": the KJV's "water of separation". The Hebrew mei niddah, "water of impurity", means the water that removes impurity. See 19:9.

31:28.t: "One out of every five hundred ... one out of every fifty": the soldiers gave less, since they had borne the risk; the community, which had not fought, gave ten times as much to the Levites.

31:29.t: "Contribution": the KJV's "heave offering", a portion lifted up and set apart for God and the priests. See Leviticus 7:14.

31:41.t: "Contribution": the KJV's "heave offering", a portion lifted up and set apart for God and the priests. See Leviticus 7:14.

31:50.t: "Armlets, bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and necklaces": the KJV's "chains, and bracelets, rings, earrings, and tablets". Several of these items cannot be identified with certainty.

"To make atonement for ourselves" (Hebrew lekhapper al-naphshotenu): to make atonement (kipper) means to remove guilt so that the relationship with God is restored, and it is related to "ransom" (kopher); see Exodus 29:33. The officers' gift may have been a ransom for the lives of the men they had counted, as in the census tax of Exodus 30:12-16, which was also "to make atonement for yourselves". It may also have been thanks that not one soldier was lost.

31:52.t: KJV: "sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels".

32:3.t: Sebam, Sibmah: the KJV spells them Shebam and Shibmah. They are probably the same town.

32:38.t: Sebam, Sibmah: the KJV spells them Shebam and Shibmah. They are probably the same town.
"These names were changed": Nebo and Baal-meon were names of gods, so Israel renamed the towns (compare Exodus 23:13).

32:12.t: Kenizzite: the KJV spells it Kenezite.

32:14.t: "A brood of sinners": the KJV's "an increase of sinful men".

32:19.t: "On this side of the Jordan, to the east": the KJV's "on this side Jordan eastward", spoken from where they stood. "On the other side of the Jordan and beyond": the KJV's "on yonder side Jordan, or forward", the land west of the river.

32:35.t: "Atroth, Shophan": the KJV's reading. Many modern Bibles read one name, Atroth-shophan. 32:35 Jazer: the KJV spells it Jaazer.

32:37.t: Kiriathaim: the KJV spells it Kirjathaim.

32:41.t: "A descendant of Manasseh": the KJV's "the son of Manasseh". Jair descended from Manasseh on his mother's side (1 Chronicles 2:21-22). Havvoth-jair means "villages of Jair"; the KJV spells it Havoth-jair.

33:1.t: "By their divisions": the KJV's "with their armies", the orderly tribal units of 2:1-34.

33:3.t: "Boldly": the KJV's "with an high hand", openly and confidently. See Exodus 14:8.

33:16.t: Most of the camps between Sinai and Kadesh are named only here, and many cannot be located today.

33:19.t: Rimmon-perez: the KJV spells it Rimmon-parez. 33:23-24 Shepher: KJV Shapher. 33:27-28 Terah, Mithkah: KJV Tarah, Mithcah. 33:32-33 Hor-haggidgad: KJV Hor-hagidgad. 33:34-35 Abronah, Ezion-geber: KJV Ebronah, Ezion-gaber. 33:44 Iye-abarim: KJV Ije-abarim; it is shortened to Iim in verse 45. 33:49 Beth-jeshimoth: KJV Beth-jesimoth.

33:49.t: Abel-shittim: "meadow of acacias", the Shittim of 25:1.

33:52.t: "Carved stones": the KJV's "pictures". The Hebrew maskit means a carved figure or image. "Cast metal idols": the KJV's "molten images".

"High places" (Hebrew bamot): hilltop shrines with altars, used in Canaanite worship and later, against the Law, in Israel as well (1 Kings 3:2, 2 Kings 23:8). Destroying them was meant to keep Israel from adopting Canaan's gods; verses 55-56 warn of what would happen otherwise, as Judges 2:1-3 records.

34:4.t: "Ascent of Akrabbim": "Scorpion Pass". The KJV's "the going forth thereof", here and in verses 5, 8, 9 and 12, means where the border ends.

34:5.t: "The Brook of Egypt": the KJV's "the river of Egypt", a seasonal stream, the Wadi el-Arish, not the Nile.

34:7.t: "Mount Hor": not the Mount Hor where Aaron died (20:22), but a mountain in the far north, probably in the Lebanon range.

34:8.t: "The entrance of Hamath": the KJV's reading. The Hebrew levo hamat may be a town, Lebo-hamath, as many modern Bibles read.

34:11.t: "Slopes": the KJV's "side", literally "shoulder". The Sea of Chinnereth is the Sea of Galilee (Luke 5:1, "the lake of Gennesaret").

34:13.t: "The nine and a half tribes": the KJV's "the nine tribes, and to the half tribe".

34:15.t: "On this side of the Jordan": the KJV's "on this side Jordan", east of the river. See 22:1.

34:18.t: "Leader": the KJV's "prince", here and in verses 22-28.

35:2.t: "Pastureland": the KJV's "suburbs", open land around a town for grazing. See Leviticus 25:34.

35:7.t: "Pastureland": the KJV's "suburbs", open land around a town for grazing. See Leviticus 25:34.

35:4.t: KJV: "a thousand cubits". 35:5 KJV: "two thousand cubits". The two measurements may describe different things: a strip about 450 meters wide around the wall, and a square about 900 meters on each side measured from outside the town.

35:6.t: "Anyone who has killed a person": the KJV's "the manslayer", "the slayer".

"Cities of refuge" (Hebrew arei miqlat, "cities of taking in"): six towns, three on each side of the Jordan, where someone who had killed a person by accident could flee. They protected him until his case was tried and kept an unintended death from starting a blood feud. Hebrews 6:18 may echo the picture when it speaks of those "who have fled for refuge" to the hope set before them.

35:11.t: "Anyone who has killed a person": the KJV's "the manslayer", "the slayer".
"By accident": the KJV's "at unawares". The Hebrew bishgagah is the word used of unintentional sins (Leviticus 4:2).

"Cities of refuge" (Hebrew arei miqlat, "cities of taking in"): six towns, three on each side of the Jordan, where someone who had killed a person by accident could flee. They protected him until his case was tried and kept an unintended death from starting a blood feud. Hebrews 6:18 may echo the picture when it speaks of those "who have fled for refuge" to the hope set before them.

35:15.t: "By accident": the KJV's "at unawares". The Hebrew bishgagah is the word used of unintentional sins (Leviticus 4:2).
"The foreigner and the resident": the KJV's "the stranger, and ... the sojourner". See Leviticus 25:23.

35:14.t: "On this side of the Jordan": east of the river. The cities are named in Deuteronomy 4:41-43 and Joshua 20:7-8.

35:20.t: "Lying in wait": the KJV's "laying of wait".

35:27.t: "Will not be guilty of bloodshed": the KJV's "shall not be guilty of blood".

35:31.t: "Ransom": the KJV's "satisfaction". The Hebrew kopher is a payment that covers a life; see Exodus 21:30, 30:12.

35:33.t: "Atonement cannot be made for the land": the KJV's "the land cannot be cleansed". The Hebrew verb is kipper, "make atonement" (Exodus 29:33).

"Pollutes the land" (Hebrew chanaph; tame): bloodshed was seen as defiling the land itself, which belonged to God and was the place where He lived among His people. Only the death of the murderer could cleanse it. Genesis 4:10 pictures Abel's blood crying out from the ground.

36:1.t: "Leaders": the KJV's "princes". "Family heads": the KJV's "chief fathers".

36:4.t: The Jubilee returned land that had been sold to its original family (Leviticus 25:13), but land that passed by inheritance through marriage would not return. The change would become permanent.

36:5.t: This completes the case of chapter 27: the daughters kept their right to inherit, and the tribe kept its land. The book ends with the new generation on the plains of Moab, ready to cross the Jordan; Deuteronomy records Moses' last words there.

36:11.t: "Their cousins on their father's side": the KJV's "their father's brothers' sons".

1:46.t: "603,550" (Hebrew elef, "thousand"): the census figures add up exactly and match the silver count of Exodus 38:26. But elef can also mean a clan or a military unit (as in "heads of thousands", 1:16, and Judges 6:15, "my clan"). Some scholars read each tribal total as so many units plus so many men (46 units, 500 men for Reuben), which gives a much smaller army. Others hold that the large numbers are meant as they stand. The KJV and most modern Bibles keep the numbers as thousands, and so do we; see Exodus 12:37.

3:12.t: "In place of every firstborn": because God spared Israel's firstborn at the Passover (Exodus 12:12-13, 13:2), every firstborn son belonged to Him. The Levites now take their place, and the 273 firstborn who outnumber the Levites are "redeemed" (Hebrew padah; see Exodus 13:13) by a payment.

5:12.t: "Goes astray" (Hebrew satah): to turn aside from the right path. The ordeal of jealousy (5:11-31) put the matter into God's hands rather than leaving a suspicious husband to act on his own. The water itself was harmless, holy water and dust, so any harm had to come from God. It protected an innocent wife as well as exposing a guilty one.

6:24.t: The priestly blessing (Hebrew birkat kohanim): these verses, the oldest known words of Scripture outside the Bible itself, were found inscribed on two small silver scrolls from about 600 BC at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem. "Bless" (barak) means to give good things and life, with God as the source. "Keep" (shamar) means to guard and watch over, as a shepherd or watchman does. "His face shine on you" (panim, "face"): the face of God means His personal presence and favor, like a king's smile toward someone he welcomes (Psalm 4:6, 80:3). "Be gracious" (chanan): to show favor to someone who has no claim on it; see Exodus 34:6. "Lift up His face toward you": the KJV's "lift up his countenance upon thee", to look on someone with attention and approval. "Peace" (shalom): see Leviticus 3:1; not only the absence of conflict but wholeness and well-being. The LORD's name is spoken three times, each line longer than the last.

6:27.t: "Put My name on the Israelites": by speaking the blessing in the LORD's name, the priests marked Israel as His people. The blessing was His, not theirs: "I will bless them."

11:17.t: "The Spirit" (Hebrew ruach): the KJV prints "spirit" in small letters, but this is the Spirit of the LORD (11:29), so we capitalize it. Ruach means spirit, wind and breath (see Genesis 1:2). God does not take away from Moses' share by giving to the elders, as one lamp lights others without losing its flame. Moses' wish in verse 29 is fulfilled at Pentecost, when Peter quotes Joel 2:28: "I will pour out My Spirit on all people" (Acts 2:17).

11:25.t: "The Spirit" (Hebrew ruach): the KJV prints "spirit" in small letters, but this is the Spirit of the LORD (11:29), so we capitalize it. Ruach means spirit, wind and breath (see Genesis 1:2). God does not take away from Moses' share by giving to the elders, as one lamp lights others without losing its flame. Moses' wish in verse 29 is fulfilled at Pentecost, when Peter quotes Joel 2:28: "I will pour out My Spirit on all people" (Acts 2:17).

"Prophesied" (Hebrew hitnabbe'u): here an outward sign of the Spirit's coming, perhaps ecstatic speech or praise, like Saul's in 1 Samuel 10:10. "Did not stop" can also be read "did not do it again"; the Hebrew is ambiguous, and many modern Bibles take it that way.

12:3.t: "Humble" (Hebrew anav): the KJV's "meek". Anav describes someone who is lowly before God and does not push himself forward, often a person who has been afflicted and relies on God rather than on his own strength. It is not weakness: Moses was a forceful leader. Here it explains why Moses did not defend himself, so God did. Psalm 37:11 promises that "the humble will inherit the land", and Jesus repeats it (Matthew 5:5). Since the verse praises Moses, many think it was added by a later hand, as was the account of his death (Deuteronomy 34).

12:7.t: "Faithful in all My house" (Hebrew ne'eman): trusted, reliable, like a steward put in charge of a whole household. Hebrews 3:2-6 quotes this verse and compares Moses, faithful as a servant in God's house, with Christ, faithful as the Son over it.

13:33.t: "Giants" (Hebrew nephilim): the same word as Genesis 6:4, where the KJV also has "giants". The spies link the descendants of Anak to the giants of old, perhaps to make them seem more frightening. "Grasshoppers" (chagavim): a small, weak insect, easy to crush. The spies' fear made them see themselves as God's enemies saw them, rather than as God saw them; compare Isaiah 40:22, where it is all the earth's people who are like grasshoppers before God.

14:18.t: Moses quotes God's own description of Himself from Exodus 34:6-7. "Slow to anger" is literally "long of nostrils", taking a long time for anger to flare; "steadfast love" is hesed, loyal covenant love that keeps its promises; and the three words for sin are avon (twisting), pesha (revolt) and chatta'ah (missing the mark). He pleads God's character as the ground for forgiveness. "Abounding in steadfast love": the KJV's "of great mercy". 14:19 "Your great steadfast love": the KJV's "the greatness of thy mercy", also hesed.

14:24.t: "Followed Me wholeheartedly" (Hebrew mille acharai, "filled after Me"): the KJV's "followed me fully". Caleb gave God undivided loyalty. The phrase becomes Caleb's mark (32:12, Joshua 14:8-14). "A different spirit" (ruach): here a person's attitude or disposition.

15:30.t: "Defiantly" (Hebrew beyad ramah, "with a high hand"): the KJV's "presumptuously". The picture is a fist raised in open defiance. Unintentional sins (bishgagah, see Leviticus 4:2) could be atoned for by sacrifice; a sin committed with a high hand was a deliberate rejection of God's authority, and the law named no sacrifice for it. The same phrase describes Israel leaving Egypt "boldly" (Exodus 14:8, 33:3), in open triumph. The man in verses 32-36 is the example that follows. Psalm 19:13 prays, "Keep Your servant also from presumptuous sins."
"Insults" (Hebrew gidduph): the KJV's "reproacheth". To sin defiantly is to revile God Himself, treating His word as worthless (15:31).

15:38.t: "Tassels" (Hebrew tsitsit): the KJV's "fringes". Tsitsit means a tuft or lock, cords knotted at the four corners of the outer garment (Deuteronomy 22:12). The "blue cord" (petil tekhelet, the KJV's "ribband of blue") used the costly dye of the priests' garments, a reminder that all Israel was called to be holy (15:40). Jewish men still wear tsitsit on the prayer shawl (tallit). The woman healed of bleeding touched the tassel of Jesus' cloak (Matthew 9:20, where the Greek kraspedon translates tsitsit), and Jesus criticized those who made their tassels long for show (Matthew 23:5).

15:39.t: "Be unfaithful" (Hebrew zonim, "go after as a prostitute"): the KJV's "go a whoring". The heart and eyes are pictured as leading a person away from God as an unfaithful spouse leaves home; see Exodus 34:15-16.

16:30.t: "The grave" (Hebrew Sheol): the KJV's "the pit". See Genesis 37:35. Sheol is the place of the dead, pictured as deep beneath the earth; going down into it "alive" stresses how sudden and direct this judgment was.

16:33.t: "The grave" (Hebrew Sheol): the KJV's "the pit". See Genesis 37:35. Sheol is the place of the dead, pictured as deep beneath the earth; going down into it "alive" stresses how sudden and direct this judgment was.

16:46.t: "Make atonement" (Hebrew kipper): to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored. The root may mean "to cover" or "to wipe clean", and it is related to "ransom" (kopher). See Exodus 29:33. Aaron, the very priest the rebels challenged, stands with his censer "between the dead and the living", and the plague stops. The scene confirms his priesthood more powerfully than any argument.

17:8.t: "Almonds" (Hebrew shaqed): the almond is the first tree to blossom in spring, and its name sounds like shaqad, "to watch" or "to be awake". Jeremiah 1:11-12 plays on the same words. The dead staff that bore buds, blossoms and ripe nuts overnight showed that life and authority come from God. The lampstand's cups were shaped like almond blossoms (Exodus 25:33).

18:19.t: "Covenant of salt": a lasting, unbreakable covenant; see Leviticus 2:13.

18:20.t: "I am your share and your inheritance" (Hebrew chelqekha venachalatekha): the priests received no land; the LORD Himself was their portion. The psalmists borrow the words: "The LORD is my chosen portion" (Psalm 16:5), "God is my portion forever" (Psalm 73:26).

19:11.t: "Dead body" (Hebrew nephesh adam): literally "the soul (or person) of a human being". Nephesh means a living, breathing creature, a whole person, and is translated soul, life, person or self depending on the setting; here it means a dead person. See Genesis 2:7.

20:10.t: Moses strikes the rock: forty years earlier God had told Moses to strike the rock (Exodus 17:6); this time he was told to speak to it. The text names the fault as unbelief, "you did not believe Me enough to show Me as holy" (Hebrew lehaqdisheni, "to treat Me as holy"). Readers have suggested several things that went wrong: Moses struck instead of speaking, struck twice, spoke in anger, and said "must we bring you water", as though the power were his and Aaron's. Psalm 106:32-33 says "he spoke rashly with his lips." Paul sees Christ in the rock that gave Israel water (1 Corinthians 10:4).

20:13.t: "Meribah" (Hebrew meribah, "quarreling") and "showed Himself holy" (Hebrew vayyiqqadesh): the place name comes from rib, "to quarrel", the verb in verse 3, as at Exodus 17:7. Kadesh, the town's name, means "holy", and the verse plays on it: at Kadesh ("holy") God showed Himself holy (qadash). This place is also called Meribah-kadesh (27:14, Deuteronomy 32:51).

21:2.t: "Devote to destruction" (Hebrew charam): the KJV's "utterly destroy". Something under herem was handed over entirely to God, either for the sanctuary or for destruction, and could not be kept for personal use. See Exodus 22:20. This is the first time Israel itself uses herem in war, as a vow to God that it would take no plunder for itself.

21:8.t: "Bronze snake" (Hebrew nechash nechoshet): the KJV's "serpent of brass". The words sound alike in Hebrew, nachash "snake" and nechoshet "bronze". The cure came not from the image itself but from trusting God's word enough to look. Centuries later Israel was burning incense to it, and Hezekiah broke it to pieces, calling it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4). Jesus said, "As Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life" (John 3:14-15).

22:20.t: Why was God angry when He had told Balaam to go? Verse 20 allowed him to go on condition that he speak only God's word; verse 22 says God was angry "because he went". Many readers take it that Balaam went with his heart set on Balak's reward (2 Peter 2:15, Jude 11), so the angel met him to make sure he understood he could say only what God told him (verse 35). Others think the story joins two accounts. Either way, the donkey sees what the paid seer cannot.

22:28.t: "The LORD opened the donkey's mouth": 2 Peter 2:16 recalls this: "a donkey that could not speak spoke with a human voice and held back the prophet's madness." The point of the story is that God controls speech: He can make a donkey speak, and He can make a hired seer bless instead of curse.

23:19.t: "God is not a man, that He should lie" (Hebrew lo ish el vikhazzev): God's word cannot fail, unlike a man's, which can be bought, as Balak hoped to buy Balaam's. "Change His mind" (Hebrew yitnecham, from nacham): the KJV's "repent". Nacham means to be sorry, grieved or moved to change course (see Genesis 6:6). 1 Samuel 15:29 repeats the thought. Where Scripture elsewhere says God relented (Exodus 32:14), it describes His response to people; here it denies that God ever goes back on what He has promised.

24:2.t: "The Spirit of God came upon him": the same words are used of judges and prophets (Judges 3:10, 1 Samuel 10:10). God spoke through Balaam even though Balaam did not serve Him faithfully; the gift does not prove the man's character (Matthew 7:22-23). The Hebrew ruach means spirit, wind and breath; see Genesis 1:2.

24:9.t: "Blessed is everyone who blesses you": Balaam repeats God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Balak hired a curse and brought one on himself.

25:3.t: "Baal of Peor" (Hebrew Ba'al Pe'or): Baal, "lord" or "master", was the Canaanite storm and fertility god, worshiped under local titles; this was the Baal of Mount Peor (23:28). "Joined in worshiping" (Hebrew tsamad, "yoked himself"): Israel bound itself to Baal as an ox is yoked. The event became a byword for apostasy (Deuteronomy 4:3, Psalm 106:28, Hosea 9:10).

25:11.t: "Zealous with My zeal ... in My jealousy" (Hebrew qanna, qin'ah): the same word means zeal and jealousy. God's jealousy is not petty envy but the rightful zeal of a husband who will not share his wife's love with another (see Exodus 20:5). Phinehas felt God's own jealous love for His people and acted on it. Psalm 106:30-31 says this "was counted to him as righteousness" (compare Genesis 15:6). The story describes a single act in a moment of judgment; it was not a pattern for private violence.

25:13.t: "Zealous with My zeal ... in My jealousy" (Hebrew qanna, qin'ah): the same word means zeal and jealousy. God's jealousy is not petty envy but the rightful zeal of a husband who will not share his wife's love with another (see Exodus 20:5). Phinehas felt God's own jealous love for His people and acted on it. Psalm 106:30-31 says this "was counted to him as righteousness" (compare Genesis 15:6). The story describes a single act in a moment of judgment; it was not a pattern for private violence.

25:12.t: "Covenant of peace" (Hebrew berit shalom): shalom means peace, wholeness, and well-being with God and others (see Leviticus 3:1). God promised Phinehas a lasting priesthood; the high priests of Solomon's temple descended from him (1 Chronicles 6:4-10). Isaiah 54:10 and Ezekiel 34:25, 37:26 use the same phrase of the covenant God would make with restored Israel.

26:55.t: "By lot" (Hebrew goral): a small stone or marked piece drawn or thrown to reach a decision. Israel understood the result as God's choice, not chance (Proverbs 16:33). The lot decided where each tribe lived; verse 54 decided how large its share was. The apostles used lots to choose Matthias (Acts 1:26).

26:64.t: Not one of those counted at Sinai was left, except Caleb and Joshua, as God had said (14:29-30). Paul uses this generation as a warning (1 Corinthians 10:5), and Hebrews 3:16-19 says they could not enter because of unbelief.

27:1.t: The daughters of Zelophehad: inheritance normally passed through sons, but these five sisters asked for their father's share, so that his name would not disappear (27:4). Moses took the case to God, who said, "The daughters of Zelophehad are right" (Hebrew ken ... dovrot, "speak rightly"), and their request became law for all Israel. Chapter 36 adds a condition, and Joshua 17:3-6 records that they received their land.

27:18.t: "A man in whom is the Spirit" (Hebrew ish asher ruach bo): the KJV prints "the spirit" in lowercase. The Hebrew says only "spirit" (ruach, which also means wind and breath; see Genesis 1:2), and it can mean God's Spirit, as at 11:17 and Genesis 41:38, or the inner gifts of courage and wisdom God had given him. Deuteronomy 34:9 says Joshua "was full of the spirit of wisdom, because Moses had laid his hands on him."

"Lay your hand on him" (Hebrew samakh, "lean on"): in the sacrifices, the worshiper pressed his hand on the animal's head, identifying himself with it (see Leviticus 1:4). Here the act passes on authority and marks Joshua publicly as Moses' successor. The apostles laid hands on those appointed to serve (Acts 6:6), and Paul on Timothy (2 Timothy 1:6).

27:23.t: "Lay your hand on him" (Hebrew samakh, "lean on"): in the sacrifices, the worshiper pressed his hand on the animal's head, identifying himself with it (see Leviticus 1:4). Here the act passes on authority and marks Joshua publicly as Moses' successor. The apostles laid hands on those appointed to serve (Acts 6:6), and Paul on Timothy (2 Timothy 1:6).

27:21.t: "Urim": the Urim and Thummim (probably "lights" and "perfections") were objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece and used to learn God's will, perhaps by giving a yes or no answer; how they worked is not described. See Exodus 28:30. Moses spoke with God face to face (12:8), but Joshua was to learn God's will through the high priest. The leader was not to act on his own judgment alone.

30:3.t: These laws protected the household. A daughter at home or a wife was under the authority of her father or husband, and a vow she made could commit the family's property or affect its life. He could cancel it, but only on the day he heard of it; if he said nothing, the vow stood, and if he canceled it later, the guilt was his. A widow or divorced woman (30:9) answered for her own vows. Hannah's vow (1 Samuel 1:11, 1:23) was made under this law.

31:2.t: "Take vengeance" (Hebrew neqam): the KJV's "avenge". In the Old Testament vengeance belongs to God (Deuteronomy 32:35); it means His just punishment of wrong, not private revenge. Here the war is called the LORD's vengeance (31:3), carried out by His command for Midian's part in leading Israel into idolatry (25:17-18). Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 in Romans 12:19 to forbid personal revenge.

32:22.t: "Free of any obligation" (Hebrew neqiyyim, "clean, innocent"): the KJV's "guiltless". The two and a half tribes could keep their land with a clear conscience once they had kept faith with their brothers. Joshua 22:1-6 records that they did.

32:23.t: "Your sin will find you out" (Hebrew chattatkhem asher timtsa etkhem): the sin itself is pictured as a pursuer that will track them down. Moses means the sin of breaking their word and abandoning their brothers: if they fail to fight, its consequences will catch up with them. The saying is often applied to hidden sins in general, which fits its spirit, though in context it is about a broken promise.

33:2.t: "Recorded" (Hebrew vayyikhtov, "wrote"): one of the few places where the Law says Moses himself wrote something down (Exodus 17:14, 24:4, 34:27, Deuteronomy 31:9). The list ties each place to what God had done there; Psalms 78 and 105 later retell the journey as a lesson in God's faithfulness.

34:2.t: "Inheritance" (Hebrew nachalah): land received as a lasting family possession, passed from parents to children. The land was God's gift and remained His (Leviticus 25:23); each family held its share as a trust. The New Testament uses the same idea of the "inheritance" believers receive in Christ (Ephesians 1:11-14, 1 Peter 1:4).

35:12.t: "Avenger of blood" (Hebrew go'el haddam): the KJV's "the revenger of blood". The go'el was the nearest male relative, responsible for his family: he redeemed land, bought back kin sold into slavery, and, when a relative was killed, put the killer to death. See Exodus 6:6 and Leviticus 25:25. The same word that names him as "kinsman-redeemer" (Ruth 3:9) names him here as avenger: both are acts of a family member restoring what was lost. The cities of refuge limited his duty to cases of deliberate murder decided by the community.

35:19.t: "Avenger of blood" (Hebrew go'el haddam): the KJV's "the revenger of blood". The go'el was the nearest male relative, responsible for his family: he redeemed land, bought back kin sold into slavery, and, when a relative was killed, put the killer to death. See Exodus 6:6 and Leviticus 25:25. The same word that names him as "kinsman-redeemer" (Ruth 3:9) names him here as avenger: both are acts of a family member restoring what was lost. The cities of refuge limited his duty to cases of deliberate murder decided by the community.

35:25.t: "Until the death of the high priest": the killer was free to go home when the high priest died. The text does not explain why. Many think the high priest's death closed the matter for the whole nation, as though his death atoned for the blood that had been shed. Some Christian readers see in it a picture of Christ, the High Priest whose death sets people free.

35:28.t: "Until the death of the high priest": the killer was free to go home when the high priest died. The text does not explain why. Many think the high priest's death closed the matter for the whole nation, as though his death atoned for the blood that had been shed. Some Christian readers see in it a picture of Christ, the High Priest whose death sets people free.

35:30.t: "Witnesses ... ransom": no one could be executed on the word of a single witness (Deuteronomy 17:6, 19:15), a rule Jesus and Paul apply to church discipline (Matthew 18:16, 2 Corinthians 13:1). Murder could not be settled with money, because a human life is not a price to be paid (Genesis 9:5-6).
